Equilibrium price. The price at which the quantity of a good that producers wish to supply exactly matches the quantity that consumers wish to demand. At this price, the market clears—there is neither surplus nor shortage. This concept forms the cornerstone of market economics, illustrating how prices coordinate production and consumption through the interaction of supply and demand.

Equilibrium price occurs at the intersection of supply and demand curves on an economic graph. It represents the price toward which a free market naturally gravitates absent artificial barriers. When the price is too low, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, creating shortage and upward pressure on price. When the price is too high, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, creating surplus and downward pressure on price. This assumes that price adjusts freely and that both buyers and sellers respond rationally to price signals.

Equilibrium is stable when small deviations from it trigger forces that restore it—a characteristic of competitive markets. However, equilibrium varies across goods and across time. Agricultural commodities may achieve equilibrium seasonally. Real markets rarely achieve perfect equilibrium due to transaction costs, information gaps, and price rigidities. Sticky prices, especially wages, prevent markets from clearing instantly. Adjustment may take weeks or months.

Price discrimination and market segmentation mean different buyers face different prices for the same good, creating multiple local equilibria. Monopolistic and oligopolistic markets may have equilibria where producers deliberately maintain prices above competitive levels to extract surplus. Despite these complications, the equilibrium price model remains fundamental to understanding how markets work.
